lessons.title: Lesson 1: The front desk job and the path to it
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the main front desk duties and the credential that can help you get hired.
This lesson builds toward: Given a front desk job posting, you will list the main front desk duties, the skills hotels ask for and a credential that matches the job, naming at least four duties and where to check the credential.
The front desk is the center of a hotel. Front desk agents (also called guest service agents) welcome guests, check them in and out, take reservations, answer the phone, handle payments and keys, solve problems and pass messages to housekeeping and maintenance. The night auditor works overnight, checks the day's numbers and closes the business day.
Hotels hire for attitude and reliability first. Postings often ask for a friendly manner, clear speaking, basic computer skills, careful cash and card handling, and the ability to work nights, weekends and holidays. A second language is a plus in many cities.
A credential can help you stand out. The American Hotel & Lodging Educational Institute (AHLEI) offers the START Certified Front Desk Representative (CFDR) online course and exam. This course prepares you for the job and for that kind of exam; it does not grant the credential. Check the AHLEI page for current details, or ask a hotel whether it pays for training. Some employers also offer apprenticeships, listed at apprenticeship.gov.
Teens: the jobs and hours you can work depend on your age and your state. Check dol.gov/youthrules and your state labor office. If you have a record, many hotels hire fairly: be honest on the application and ready to talk about what you have done since.
Words to know:
- Front desk agent: the hotel worker who checks guests in and out and helps them during their stay; also called a guest service agent.
- Night auditor: the overnight front desk worker who checks the day's charges and payments and closes the business day.
- Credential: a certificate that shows you passed a course or exam.
- AHLEI: the American Hotel & Lodging Educational Institute, which offers hotel training and certification exams.
Official sources:
- AHLEI: START Certified Front Desk Representative (CFDR) Online Course and Exam
- AHLEI: certification exams
- Apprenticeship.gov (US Department of Labor)
- YouthRules! (US Department of Labor)
Try it now: Find one real front desk or guest service agent posting near you (a job site or a hotel's careers page). On paper, list four duties it names, three skills it asks for, and the shift times. Circle one skill you already have and one you need to build.
You can now say what a front desk agent does, name the skills hotels ask for, and name a credential that can help and where to check it.

check.q: Which is a normal front desk duty?
options: Fixing the air conditioner in a room
Cooking breakfast for guests
Checking guests in and out
Cleaning the pool
check.why: Check-in and check-out are core front desk work; repairs, cooking and cleaning belong to other teams.

check.q: What does this course do for the CFDR credential?
options: It grants the CFDR certificate
It prepares you; you earn the credential through AHLEI's course and exam
It replaces the need for any training
It is the same as a state license
check.why: AHLEI grants the CFDR after its own course and exam; this course only prepares you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Checking a guest in
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check in a practice guest in seven steps, from greeting to key.
This lesson builds toward: Given a practice guest with a reservation, you will check the guest in step by step, from greeting to handing over the key, without skipping a step and without saying the room number out loud.
Check-in is the guest's first real moment with the hotel. Do it in the same order every time so nothing gets missed, even when there is a line.
Greet the guest, find the reservation and check the photo ID matches the name. Confirm the dates, room type and rate. Take the payment card, or a deposit by the hotel's rules; many hotels place a hold on the card for the stay and extra charges, and you explain that in plain words.
Give the key card and point to the room on the key folder or a slip, but do not say the room number out loud: other people in the lobby can hear. Explain the basics (Wi-Fi, breakfast, check-out time) and ask if they need anything else.
Every hotel uses a computer system, called a property management system (PMS), to record all of this. Systems differ, and the hotel will train you on its own; the steps stay the same.
Step by step:
- Greet the guest with a smile and your name.
- Find the reservation and check the photo ID matches it.
- Confirm the dates, room type and rate.
- Take the payment card or deposit and explain any hold.
- Make the key card and write the room number on the key folder; do not say it aloud.
- Explain Wi-Fi, breakfast and check-out time.
- Ask "Is there anything else I can help with?" and wish them a good stay.
Words to know:
- Reservation: a booking that holds a room for a guest for certain dates.
- Rate: the price per night for the room.
- Hold (authorization): an amount the hotel holds on a guest's card to cover the stay and extra charges; it is not the final charge.
- Property management system (PMS): the hotel's computer system for reservations, rooms, check-in, bills and check-out.
Try it now: With a friend or in a mirror, check in a made-up guest: "Ms. Rivera, two nights, one king room." Say all seven steps out loud. Write room 214 on a paper key folder and point to it instead of saying it. Do it twice, the second time in under three minutes.
You can now check in a guest in seven steps and hand over the key without saying the room number out loud.

check.q: You are handing a guest the key. What do you do with the room number?
options: Say it loudly so they remember
Tell the whole line so they know
Text it to the guest's friend
Write it on the key folder and point to it
check.why: Saying the room number aloud lets strangers in the lobby know where the guest is staying.

check.q: What do you check right after finding the reservation?
options: That the photo ID matches the name on the reservation
The guest's job
How the guest got to the hotel
The guest's home address on social media
check.why: Matching the ID to the reservation makes sure the room goes to the right person.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reading the folio and checking a guest out
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain each charge on a guest folio and check the guest out.
This lesson builds toward: Given a practice guest folio at check-out, you will explain each charge on the folio and check the guest out, with every charge explained and any wrong charge sent to a manager or fixed by the rules.
A folio is the guest's bill. It lists every night's room rate, taxes and any extra charges, such as parking, room service, a mini-bar or a late check-out fee, and every payment.
At check-out, greet the guest, ask how the stay was, and print or email the folio. Go over it line by line if the guest wants, and listen to anything that was wrong with the stay.
If the guest questions a charge, stay calm and look at it together. If it is a clear mistake the hotel lets you fix, fix it and say so. If you are not allowed to remove it, say "Let me get my manager so we can sort this out," and do not argue. Many hotels also offer express check-out by phone, TV or app.
Protect card details: never write down or read out a full card number. Folios show only the last few digits.
Step by step:
- Greet the guest and ask how the stay was.
- Print or email the folio.
- Go over each charge if the guest asks.
- Fix a clear mistake if your hotel allows it; otherwise call the manager.
- Take the final payment, thank the guest and invite them back.
Words to know:
- Folio: the guest's bill, listing room charges, taxes, extras and payments.
- Incidentals: extra charges during a stay, like parking, food or phone calls.
- Late check-out: leaving after the normal check-out time, sometimes for a fee.
- Express check-out: checking out without stopping at the desk, by phone, TV or app.
Try it now: Make a practice folio on paper for a made-up guest: two nights at $129, tax shown as a separate line (use any made-up amount), parking $15 each night, and one $12 room service charge that the guest says they did not order. Add it up, then write what you would say about each line and how you would handle the room service charge.
You can now read a folio line by line, explain each charge, and handle a questioned charge calmly by the hotel's rules.

options: The guest's room key
The guest's bill with charges and payments
A list of hotel rules
The housekeeping schedule
check.why: The folio lists every room charge, tax, extra and payment for the stay.

check.q: A guest questions a charge you are not allowed to remove. What do you say?
options: "Too bad, you have to pay it."
"I will just delete it."
"Let me get my manager so we can sort this out."
"Call your bank."
check.why: Calling a manager keeps you calm and inside the rules, and gets the guest an answer.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Problems, privacy and your shift

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Solving guest problems, even when the hotel is full
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Solve a guest problem with an apology, two choices and a follow-up note.
This lesson builds toward: Given an upset guest or a full hotel, you will solve the guest's problem with an apology, choices and a follow-up note, staying calm and giving the guest at least two choices.
Things go wrong in hotels: a room is not ready, the air conditioning is loud, a reservation is missing. The guest is tired and wants a fix. Your job is to stay calm, own the problem and offer choices.
Use four moves: listen without interrupting, apologize ("I'm sorry, that's not the stay we want for you"), offer at least two choices (another room, a fix by a certain time, a manager's offer), then follow up and write it in the shift log so the next shift knows.
Sometimes a hotel is overbooked and a guest with a reservation has no room. Hotels may "walk" the guest: book them at a nearby hotel. Follow your hotel's walk policy and get a manager. Never promise money or free nights you are not allowed to give.
If a guest yells, threatens or becomes unsafe, you do not have to handle it alone. Step back and call your manager or security.
Step by step:
- Listen to the whole problem without interrupting.
- Apologize and thank the guest for telling you.
- Offer at least two choices you are allowed to give.
- Do what you promised, or get a manager.
- Follow up with the guest and write it in the shift log.
Words to know:
- Overbooked: when the hotel has more reservations than rooms.
- Walking a guest: booking a guest who cannot get a room at another nearby hotel, by the hotel's policy.
- Shift log: a written or computer log where the front desk records problems and messages for the next shift.
Try it now: Write what you would say to this guest: "I booked a room with two beds and you gave me one king. My kids are with me." Write your apology, two choices you could offer, and the one-line note you would put in the shift log. Then say it out loud.
You can now calm an upset guest, offer two choices, follow up and log the problem, and know when to get a manager.

check.q: A guest's room is not ready. Which reply follows the four moves?
options: "Not my fault, come back later."
"Rooms are never ready on time."
"Here is a free week."
"I'm sorry. I can store your bags and call you by 3 pm, or check for another room now."
check.why: It apologizes and offers two choices the agent can give.

check.q: The hotel is overbooked and a guest has no room. What do you do?
options: Follow the walk policy and get a manager
Tell the guest to sleep in the lobby
Promise a refund for a whole month
Cancel another guest's room without asking
check.why: Walking a guest by policy, with a manager, is how hotels handle overbooking fairly.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Guest privacy, keys and safety
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Respond to privacy, key and safety situations by the hotel's rules.
This lesson builds toward: Given a privacy, safety or emergency situation at the desk, you will respond by the hotel's safety and privacy rules, never giving out a guest's room number or key, and calling 911 or a manager when needed.
Guest privacy keeps people safe. Never tell a caller or visitor whether someone is staying at the hotel or what room they are in. Say "I can't share guest information, but I can connect you to the room if the guest is staying here" or take a message. Never give a key to someone whose name is not on the room without the hotel's ID process.
Key cards: check ID before making a new key, never leave key cards or the key machine where guests can reach them, and report lost master keys at once.
Service animals: under the ADA, when it is not obvious, staff may ask only two questions: is the dog required because of a disability, and what work or task has it been trained to perform. You cannot ask for papers or charge a pet fee for a service animal.
Watch for signs of human trafficking, such as a person who seems controlled by someone else, coached on what to say or afraid. Do not confront anyone. Tell your manager and follow hotel policy; you can report to the National Human Trafficking Hotline at 1-888-373-7888. In any emergency (fire, medical, violence), call 911 (or your local emergency number) first, then your manager.
Step by step:
- Never confirm a guest is staying or share a room number.
- Offer to connect the call to the room or take a message.
- Check ID before making any new key.
- For a service animal, ask only the two allowed questions when needed.
- Report trafficking signs to your manager; do not confront anyone.
- In an emergency, call 911 first, then your manager.
Words to know:
- Key control: the rules for making, storing and tracking room keys so only the right people get in.
- ADA: the Americans with Disabilities Act, the US law that protects people with disabilities, including their use of service animals.
- Service animal: under the ADA, a dog trained to do work or tasks for a person with a disability.
- Human trafficking: using force, fraud or threats to make someone work or do sex acts.
Official sources:
- ADA.gov: ADA Requirements: Service Animals
- DHS Blue Campaign: Indicators of Human Trafficking
- AHLA Foundation: No Room For Trafficking (free hotel staff training)
Try it now: Write your answer to each: (1) A caller says "Put me through to my wife, Jane Lee. What room is she in?" (2) A man without ID says he lost his key to room 305. (3) A guest has a dog; you are not sure it is a service animal. Then, if you can, take the free 30-minute "Your Role in Preventing Human Trafficking" training linked from the AHLA Foundation's No Room For Trafficking page.
You can now protect guest privacy on the phone and at the desk, control keys, handle a service animal by the ADA, and report trafficking signs and emergencies the right way.

check.q: A caller asks what room a guest is in. What do you say?
options: Give the room number
"I can't share guest information, but I can connect you or take a message."
"She checked out an hour ago."
"Call back when I'm off shift."
check.why: Never confirm a guest is staying or share a room number; connecting or taking a message protects the guest.

check.q: A guest has a dog and it is not obvious it is a service animal. What may you ask?
options: For the dog's certification papers
What the guest's disability is
To pay the pet fee first
Whether the dog is required for a disability and what task it is trained to do
check.why: The ADA allows only those two questions; no papers and no pet fee for a service animal.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your shift checklist and your job plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a front desk shift checklist and a 30-day plan toward a front desk job.
This lesson builds toward: Given a front desk job posting, you will list the main front desk duties, the skills hotels ask for and a credential that matches the job, naming at least four duties and where to check the credential. Given a practice guest with a reservation, you will check the guest in step by step, from greeting to handing over the key, without skipping a step and without saying the room number out loud.
Good front desk agents work from a checklist. At the start of a shift: arrive early, read the shift log, count your cash drawer with a manager or by the hotel's process, and check today's arrivals, departures and rooms ready.
During the shift: greet every guest, check in and out with the same steps, answer the phone by the third ring if you can, keep the desk neat and keep keys secure. At the end: finish open tasks, count your drawer again, and write anything the next shift must know in the log.
Now plan your path. Pick three hotels near you, practice your check-in script with a real person, and decide when you will look at the AHLEI CFDR page or ask an employer if it pays for training. Put real dates on each step. Bring your checklist and script to the interview: it shows you already know the job.
Step by step:
- Write the start-of-shift tasks.
- Write the during-shift tasks.
- Write the end-of-shift tasks.
- Write your check-in script with the privacy rule in it.
- Write a 30-day plan with dates: three hotels, practice, and the credential check.
Words to know:
- Cash drawer (bank): the cash a front desk agent is responsible for during a shift; it is counted at the start and end.
- Arrivals and departures: the lists of guests checking in and checking out today.
- Shift handoff: passing on open tasks and notes to the next shift.
Try it now: Build your job kit on paper or in a free document: your shift checklist (start, during, end), your check-in script in seven steps, and a 30-day plan with real dates. Ask someone to play the guest while you read the script.
You can now show a hiring manager a front desk shift checklist, a check-in script and a dated plan toward the job and a credential.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Shift checklist The checklist is missing the start, middle or end of the shift. It has start, during and end tasks, including the shift log and the drawer count. It also adds key control and phone tasks and fits on one clear page. Check-in script Steps are missing or the script says the room number out loud. All seven steps in order, with the room number written and pointed to, not said. Read aloud to a partner in under three minutes, with a warm greeting and close. Folio and check-out Cannot explain the charges, or would argue about a questioned charge. Explains each charge on a practice folio and says to fix a clear mistake or get a manager. Also explains a card hold in plain words and never shows a full card number. Problem solving The reply argues, blames or promises what the agent cannot give. Apologizes, offers at least two allowed choices and writes a shift log note. Also says when to get a manager and how they would follow up with the guest. Privacy and safety Shares a room number, gives a key without ID, or would confront a suspected trafficker. Protects guest information, checks ID for keys, and reports emergencies and trafficking signs correctly. Also handles a service animal with only the two ADA questions and has taken a free trafficking training. 30-day plan No dates, or no named hotels. Three named hotels, a practice date and a date to check the CFDR page or ask about training. Also lists who will be a reference and how they will get to each shift. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which belongs in a 30-day front desk job plan?
options: "Someday look for jobs"
"Apply to three named hotels by the 15th and practice my script on the 10th"
"Pay someone for a guaranteed job"
"Wait for a hotel to call me"
check.why: A real plan names specific steps with dates.

check.q: What is a good start-of-shift task?
options: Read the shift log and check today's arrivals
Leave the drawer uncounted
Turn off the phones
Give out spare keys to save time
check.why: Reading the log and arrivals tells you what the shift needs before guests arrive.
